summary: This standards-track document gives definitions, originally in RFC 1494, for carrying CCITT G3 fax in MIME and translating it to its X.400 representation.

eli5.summary: Packaging a fax so it can travel in email.

subtitle: How to carry a Group 3 fax inside a MIME email message, and map it to and from X.400.

tldr.problem: Fax pages needed a standard way to travel inside Internet mail and to be translated to the X.400 fax body part used by other mail systems.
tldr.mechanism: The image/g3fax content-type carries the T.4 bit stream unchanged, with fax settings as MIME parameters and six end-of-line markers between pages.
tldr.outcome: Fax data can move between MIME and X.400 in a reversible way. The RFC itself says the format is not a general-purpose Internet image format.

facts.label: Page delimiter
facts.value: 6 EOLs, starting on a byte boundary

today: RFC 2159 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself describes the format as only for carrying data already in G3 Fax form.

sections.title: Why a Fax Body Part
sections.content:
RFC 2159 holds the definitions, originally in RFC 1494, on how to carry CCITT G3Fax in MIME and how to translate it to its X.400 representation.

The author adds a warning. The format does not seem appropriate as a general purpose image format for the Internet. It exists only to carry information that is already in G3 Fax format, which may be usefully converted to other formats in specific contexts.
sections.eli5: This is a way to mail a fax as it is, not a new picture format. If you want a normal picture, convert it afterwards.

sections.title: The image/g3fax Content-Type
sections.content:
The image/g3fax content-type carries G3 Facsimile byte streams. A G3Fax image holds three pieces of information.

  • Flags that say which coding scheme is used. T.30 defines how they are sent over telephones; here they are parameters in the MIME content-type header field.
  • A structure that divides the bits into pages. The T.4 "return to command mode" string marks page breaks.
  • For each page, the bits that encode the image. T.4 defines this bit image format and it is used without change. The highest bit of the first byte is the first bit of the T.4 bitstream.
sections.eli5: A fax in an email has three parts: a list of settings, a mark between pages, and the dots that make up each page.

sections.title: G3Fax Parameters
sections.content:
Six parameters are defined.

  • page-length: A4, B4 or Unlimited.
  • page-width: A3, A4 or B4.
  • encoding: 1-dimensional, 2-dimensional or Uncompressed.
  • resolution: Fine or Coarse.
  • DCS: a bit string, represented in Base64.
  • pages: an integer giving the number of pages in the document.

If nothing is specified, the defaults are page-length A4, page-width A4, 1-dimensional encoding and Coarse resolution.

The values can be viewed as single-bit flags, which the RFC calls possible but misleading. They map to bits of the T.30 control string and of the X.400 G3FacsimileParameters. X.400 counts bits in an octet from the most significant bit down, while T.30 uses the opposite numbering, so the numbers differ. If any other bit is set in the Device Control String, the DCS parameter should be supplied.
sections.eli5: The settings say how big the paper is, how the dots are squeezed, and how sharp the picture is. If nothing is said, plain defaults are used.

sections.title: Content Encoding and Page Breaks
sections.content:
X.400 defines the g3-facsimile data stream as a SEQUENCE of BIT STRINGs, one per page. The MIME encoding is reversible with it and makes sure page breaks are honored.

An EOL is the bit sequence 000000000001 (eleven zeroes and a one). Each page is delimited by a sequence of six EOLs that MUST start on a byte boundary. The image bit stream is padded with zeroes as needed to achieve that alignment.

To find a page boundary, search for the byte sequence (hex) 00 10 01 00 10 01 00 10 01, which cannot occur inside the image. The Base64 content-transfer-encoding is appropriate for carrying this content-type.
sections.eli5: Between pages there is a special row of six marker beeps. The padding makes sure the marker starts at a clean spot, so it is easy to find.

sections.title: Converting To and From X.400
sections.content:
The X.400 body part is g3-facsimile and the MIME type is image/g3fax. The conversion type is nearly a byte copy, and the X.400 parameters map to the MIME parameters and back.

Going from X.400 to G3Fax: trailing EOL markers on each bitstring are removed, the bit order is changed so the highest bit of the first byte is the first bit, and the bitstring is padded to a byte boundary. Six consecutive EOL markers are appended to each one, and the padded strings are concatenated.

Going from G3Fax to X.400: the body is split at each occurrence of six consecutive EOL markers. Trailing EOLs must NOT be removed, because the X.400 Implementor Guide recommends that each page end with six EOLs, a change from RFC 1494. Each piece becomes an ASN.1 BITSTRING with the bit order within each byte reversed, and the pieces form an ASN.1 SEQUENCE.

Two cautions apply. If fineResolution is not specified, pixels will be twice as tall as they are wide. If any bit without a specially named option is set in the NonBasicParameters, the DCS parameter must be used, and interworking is not guaranteed.
sections.eli5: Turning a mailed fax into the other mail system's kind means cutting it at the six-marker spots, flipping the order of the dots in each byte, and stacking the pages in a list. Going back is the reverse.

sections.title: Practical Guidance on Usability
sections.content:
This section is not part of the proposed standard. It is guidance for implementors.

The DCS bit string is long. The T.30 Recommendation (1993) gives 67 bits with specific functions, SG8 Report R33 extends this to 75 bits, and Report R41 (approved in 1995) extends it to 79 bits. No sane implementor will send such things without being able to negotiate them down, but messages with such bits set could still arrive through X.400.

The ISO P2 profile from 1995 makes reception of two-dimensional and fine-resolution mandatory if g3-facsimile is supported at all. Research by Andrew Gordon of Net-Tel indicates that fine resolution, unlimited length and B4 length are easy for an access unit to support, B4 width is nearly impossible, and A3 width is hard. Some fax machines also have trouble if scan lines do not contain exactly the declared number of pixels, so omitting right-hand white space is likely to cause trouble.
sections.eli5: Some fax settings are easy for a machine to handle and some are very hard. Machines should not skip the blank space at the end of a line, because some fax machines get confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that there are no known security issues specific to the FAX body part. It adds no other security guidance.
sections.eli5: The authors did not know of any special danger in mailing faxes this way.
